title: From Points to Obstacles: Clustering by Distance, With a Radius That Grows With Range Because the Points Do

questions.question: What is the one parameter that decides a clustering by distance?
options: How many points a cluster must have
How many beams the sensor has
How far the scene is from the sensor
How close two points must be to be one thing
questions.explanation: Points closer than the radius are joined, and chains of joined points are one group. Everything else follows from that distance.

questions.question: At a radius of 0.2 m the scene gave:
questions.explanation: The post, the person and the two posts 0.8 m apart came out as four, and the three scattered points were dropped for having too few neighbours.

questions.question: At a radius of 5 m the scene gave:
questions.explanation: At 5 m every point is within reach of some other, so the whole scene is one object. At 0.6 m the two posts had already joined.

questions.question: A fixed radius of 0.15 m on a wall 11 m away found how many objects?
questions.explanation: At 11 m with one degree between beams the points are 0.19 m apart. With a radius of 0.15 m no two join, and single points are dropped.

questions.question: Why does the radius grow with range?
options: The points of a far thing are further apart
The sensor's beams are wider at range
questions.explanation: The spacing of the points is the range times the beam step. A radius of a base plus one and a half times that spacing held the far wall together.

questions.question: What does a radius that is the same at every range do near the sensor?
options: It joins things that are close together, like two posts with a gap between them
It splits one object into many
questions.explanation: Two posts 0.35 m apart at 2 m became one object with a radius of 0.4 m. A radius that grows with range kept them as two.
